entries.question: Why does test/integration/profile-form.test.ts read the $ACTION_ field index out of the rendered /profile page and scope its read to one form, when spec 0010's build plan says to confirm the fields $ACTION_REF_1 / $ACTION_1:0 / $ACTION_1:1 are present?
entries.why_multiple_records: Spec 0010 holds the stale value (index 1) in its build plan, unmarked, and names the identity form on /profile as the one action driven without a browser. The correction, and the reason a second form on the same page shifts the index, live only in spec 0004's Follow up, which also records why the technique was deferred to feature 9 in the first place. Reading 0010 alone gives the wrong field names; reading 0004 alone does not say which form or page the test drives.

trace.record: spec 0004 Follow-up (Server Action without a browser)
trace.quote: **Driving a Server Action without a browser is deferred to feature 9, deliberately.** [...] It is deferred rather than met because there is nothing honest to drive yet: the only Server Action in the repository is `signInWithDevPassword`, which feature 7 deletes, and the first real write path is feature 9's profile form.

The identity save Server Action, as this feature's representative write path, is driven once from a test with no browser [...]: fetch the page with the edit form open, read the rendered form's hidden action fields, and post them back; a redirect carrying the session cookie means it ran.

Before building the other four forms, spike the `useActionState` hidden field shape spec 0004's Follow up recipe assumes: render the identity form, fetch the page, confirm `$ACTION_REF_1` / `$ACTION_1:0` / `$ACTION_1:1` / `$ACTION_KEY` are present in the HTML.

**`<n>` is a per form index, not part of the name, corrected on 2026 09 02 when feature 9 proved this against React 19.2.8 and Next.js 16.3.1.** This wording said `1` until then, which is wrong on any page carrying more than one form: `/profile` renders the identity form as `$ACTION_REF_2`, because the signed in header's sign out form is numbered first. Read the index out of the rendered page rather than assuming it, and scope the read to the one form under test, or the sign out action's own field is harvested and posted alongside.

also.quote: Action ids come from `.next/server/server-reference-manifest.json`, and an id is only valid for a build made at that same directory path, so an id read locally is the wrong id on Vercel.

corroboration.quote: there is no way to stage that over HTTP, because the page is the only thing that hands out the action id.

entries.answer: The recipe was written in spec 0004 before any real form existed (the only action was the dev password sign in, due for deletion), so it assumed index 1. Spec 0010's identity form on /profile was the first real target, and its build plan copied that assumption. On /profile, though, the signed in header's sign out form is numbered first, so the identity form renders as $ACTION_REF_2. The test therefore reads the index from the rendered page and scopes the read to the identity form, or it would also harvest and post the sign out action's field. Spec 0004 recorded the correction on 2026 09 02; spec 0010's build step still says 1.

entries.question: Why does spec 0018 say to read a pair's `distribution` and never its `summary` when asking how the five reruns split, given that spec 0017 requires every verdict to carry a count like '5 of 5 succeeded'?
entries.why_multiple_records: Spec 0017 explains what the count is and why it is mandatory: it is the success denominator, so a verdict resting on 3 successes can be told apart from one resting on 5. Spec 0018 records that the same count was read as a band tally, which produced a false 'stable at 5 of 5' claim, and gives the real splits. Reading 0017 alone, the format looks unambiguous. Reading 0018 alone, the misread looks like carelessness rather than a property of the format.

trace.quote: A pair's verdict needs at least 3 of its 5 reruns to be scored successes; with fewer than 3, the pair is `inconclusive` (sub reason `insufficient-successes`) [...] compute how many of the successes landed on each band. If one band holds a strict majority (more than half of the successes), that is the pair's verdict band

Every printed and reported verdict names its own denominator (e.g. "good_match, 3 of 3 succeeded" or, for a distribution shaped verdict, "3 strong_match / 2 possible_match, 5 of 5 succeeded"), never just a band on its own, so a reader can tell a verdict resting on the minimum 3 successes apart from one resting on all 5, and can see a split even where the pair still passed.
per pair, its status (`pass`/`fail`/`inconclusive`), sub reason where relevant, denominator, and every observed band (or band distribution)

A caution that belongs in the record, because it caused a wrong conclusion once already. The report's `summary` field reads like `"possible_match, 5 of 5 succeeded"`, and the `5 of 5` there is the **success denominator**, meaning all five reruns returned a band rather than failing. It is not the count landing on that band. Reading it as the band count is what produced the claim that both pairs were stable at 5 of 5, which the distributions above disprove. Read `distribution`, never `summary`, when the question is how the reruns split.
The correction states the per pair distributions rather than a summary line, removes the "stable disagreement" inference, and points at this spec.

The report's `summary` field is easy to misread as a band count when it is a success denominator, and it caused a wrong conclusion in this spec's own first draft. Worth considering whether `formatReportTable` and the JSON should make the distribution the prominent value, since the distribution is what anyone reasoning about a disagreement actually needs.

entries.answer: Spec 0017 made every verdict carry 'N of 5 succeeded' on purpose. N counts reruns that returned any band, as opposed to failing, so a reader can tell a verdict resting on the 3-success floor from one resting on all 5. It does not count how many reruns landed on the verdict band, which only needs a strict majority of successes. Spec 0018 found that reading the count as a band tally produced the claim that two pairs were stable at 5 of 5. The per pair distributions, which the report records separately, showed 1 to 4 and 3 to 2 splits on the first run. So 0018 tells readers to use `distribution`, corrected the recorded evidence to state distributions, and left open a follow up to make the distribution the prominent value in the report.

entries.question: control-one-gap passed its confirming run by only 3 to 2 (possible_match over good_match). Why can't it be given acceptableBands [good_match, possible_match] so it stops sitting one rerun away from having no majority?
entries.why_multiple_records: What acceptableBands is for, and what the control tag means, are both defined in spec 0016. The finding that the anchors settle this pair, the refusal to widen it, and the test that now ties the tag to the tolerance are in spec 0018. Why 3 to 2 is the narrowest possible pass is in spec 0017's verdict rule. No single record shows that both obvious ways out are closed.

trace.record: spec 0016 Key invariants, what acceptableBands is for
trace.quote: `acceptableBands`, when present, always includes its own `expectedBand` and holds at least two bands; it is used only where the anchor text itself cannot honestly narrow to one band (AC-3), never as a way to avoid reasoning a pair through carefully.

trace.record: spec 0016 pair table, what the control tag means
trace.quote: `possible_match`'s own anchor names exactly this shape with no ambiguity, unlike `boundary-seniority-gap` above, which is why this pair carries no `acceptableBands` and the plain `control` tag rather than `boundary`.
**Finding 1, `control-one-gap` is a wrong expectation, and the anchors already settle it.** [...] `possible_match`'s existing text is a better fit with no new rule needed
`acceptableBands` widens a genuine ambiguity in the anchors. It is not a way to stop a pair failing, which is why `control-one-gap` is corrected outright rather than given a tolerance.

If one band holds a strict majority (more than half of the successes), that is the pair's verdict band, and the pair passes if that band equals `expectedBand`, or, when `acceptableBands` is present, if it is one of them.
`possible_match` won it 4 to 1, then 5 to 0, then 3 to 2 on the confirming run

retagging it `boundary` would concede that the anchors do not settle it, which contradicts this spec's own finding that they do, and widening it with `acceptableBands` is refused outright by the Key invariants above. `ground-truth.test.ts` now asserts that no `control` tagged pair carries `acceptableBands`, so the retag and the tolerance are not independent choices.

entries.answer: Spec 0016 allows acceptableBands only where the anchor text cannot narrow a pair to one band, and uses the control tag for pairs whose anchor text settles them with no ambiguity. Spec 0018 found the anchors do settle control-one-gap at possible_match, so a tolerance would cover up a mistake rather than record an ambiguity. Its invariant refuses that outright. ground-truth.test.ts now asserts that no control-tagged pair carries acceptableBands, so a tolerance would also force a retag to boundary, which would contradict 0018's own finding. That is why the pair stays exact and fragile. Under 0017's strict majority rule, 3 to 2 is the narrowest pass possible: one rerun landing on good_match instead makes good_match the majority and fails the pair, and one rerun failing at the vendor leaves a 2 to 2 split with no majority, which is inconclusive. Spec 0018 records whether the pair should keep its control tag as an open question, not a decided one.
entries.confidence_note: Every quote was read directly. Did not open ground-truth.test.ts or pairs.ts, so the claim that the no-control-with-acceptableBands assertion exists rests on 0018 line 106. The fragility point is arithmetic from 0017 AC-3: 3 good_match to 2 possible_match is a good_match majority and fails the pair; 2 to 2 of 4 successes has no majority and is inconclusive. 0018 verify.md line 45 says one flipped rerun 'would leave no majority at all', which contradicts AC-3.

entries.question: Why does band-anchors.test.ts pin BAND_ANCHORS twice, once as five inline strings and once as bandAnchorsHash(BAND_ANCHORS), when either assertion alone fails on an anchor edit?
entries.why_multiple_records: Spec 0016 explains why drift matters (every expected band is derived from today's wording, and that wording 'is expected to change') and records how the two assertions were shown to be separate. Spec 0017 makes the hash a field in every eval report and requires the report writer and the test to share one function. Spec 0018 is the first record that relies on the hash staying put to compare reports before and after a change. Without 0017 the hash assertion looks redundant. Without 0016 the guard has no stated purpose.

trace.record: spec 0016 Follow-up, anchor drift (requested, then done)
trace.quote: `BAND_ANCHORS`'s own comment (`rubric.ts:63-67`) states its wording "is expected to change". Every `expectedBand` and `rationale` in this set is derived from today's wording.

also.quote: A second assertion pins `bandAnchorsHash(BAND_ANCHORS)`, which is the value written into every eval report, so a change to the hash function alone is caught as well; the two were proved distinct by changing only the separator, which fails the hash assertion while the text one still passes.

trace.quote: As the person reading a report later, I want it to record which model and which rubric wording it was measured against, so a report from three weeks ago can tell "the scorer changed" apart from "the rubric changed".

trace.record: spec 0017 AC-9, the hash in the report
trace.quote: a hash of `BAND_ANCHORS`'s current text (`bandAnchorsHash()`, defined once and shared with the AC-10 test, so "the same way" is true by construction rather than by two separate implementations agreeing).

A committed test (no vendor call, runs under the ordinary free unit suite) asserts `BAND_ANCHORS` literally equals today's text (`toEqual` against the five strings written inline in the test, never a snapshot file, which a routine `vitest -u` could silently rewrite) and that `bandAnchorsHash(BAND_ANCHORS)` equals today's computed hash

trace.record: spec 0018 AC-2, the hash relied on
trace.quote: `BAND_ANCHORS` in `src/features/scoring/rubric.ts` is unchanged, so `band-anchors.test.ts`'s pinned text and committed hash `1b45f524b356` are untouched and still pass, and reports written before and after this change remain comparable.

corroboration.quote: `bandAnchorsHash(BAND_ANCHORS)`, unchanged at `1b45f524b356` because the anchors are untouched, which is what keeps this change's runs comparable with the two baseline runs.

entries.answer: The two assertions protect two different things. The ground truth pairs were argued from today's anchor wording, and that wording is expected to change (0016). The inline text pin catches a wording edit at commit time, in the free unit suite. It uses inline strings rather than a snapshot because 'vitest -u' could silently rewrite a snapshot (0017 AC-10). The hash is also the value written into every eval report, so a reader can tell 'the rubric changed' apart from 'the scorer changed' (0017 user story, AC-9). The report writer and the test share one bandAnchorsHash() function, and pinning the hash catches a change to that function even when the text is unchanged. Changing only the separator showed the two assertions are separate: the hash assertion fails while the text assertion still passes (0016). Spec 0018 is where this pays off. It corrected a pair rather than the anchors, and the unchanged hash 1b45f524b356 is how it shows that reports from before and after the correction can still be compared.
